sveltekit.description: My go-to framework for building fast, full-stack web apps — this site is built with it.
sveltekit.pro: Ships almost no runtime — components compile down to tight vanilla JS, so pages stay small and fast by default.
sveltekit.contra: Smaller ecosystem than React means fewer ready-made libraries and community answers for edge cases.

typescript.description: My default for anything beyond a quick script — types catch mistakes long before they hit production.
typescript.pro: Catches whole categories of bugs at compile time and makes refactoring large codebases far less scary.
typescript.contra: Build step and type-fighting add real friction, especially with loosely-typed third-party libraries.

javascript.description: The language everything else on the web is built on — I still reach for it directly when TypeScript is overkill.
javascript.pro: Runs everywhere without a build step and has the largest ecosystem of any language on earth.
javascript.contra: No types by default means bugs that TypeScript would catch instantly slip through until runtime.

tailwind.description: How I style almost everything now — utility classes right in the markup, no context-switching to a stylesheet.
tailwind.pro: Fast to build and change UI with, and the design stays consistent since you're picking from a fixed scale.
tailwind.contra: Markup gets noisy with long class strings, and it takes a while to learn where the useful defaults are.

rust.description: My pick when performance and correctness actually matter — the compiler is strict, but it's strict for good reason.
rust.pro: Memory safety without a garbage collector, plus a compiler that catches concurrency bugs before they ship.
rust.contra: Steep learning curve — the borrow checker fights you constantly until the ownership model clicks.

cpp.description: Where I go for raw performance and low-level control, especially in resource-constrained environments.
cpp.pro: Extremely fast, gives you direct control over memory and hardware, and still runs almost everywhere.
cpp.contra: Manual memory management is easy to get wrong, and compile times/tooling lag behind newer languages.

java.description: Solid, boring-in-a-good-way — reliable for backend services that need to run unattended for years.
java.pro: Mature ecosystem, strong tooling, and the JVM's stability make it a safe long-term bet for big systems.
java.contra: Verbose compared to newer languages, and startup/memory overhead can be heavy for small services.

go.description: My choice for backend services and CLI tools where simplicity and fast builds matter more than expressiveness.
go.pro: Compiles fast, deploys as a single binary, and its concurrency model (goroutines) is genuinely pleasant.
go.contra: Deliberately minimal — no generics-heavy patterns or exceptions means more boilerplate in places.

react.description: I know it well and reach for it when a project already lives in that ecosystem or needs its library depth.
react.pro: Huge ecosystem and hiring pool — almost any problem already has a well-tested library for it.
react.contra: More boilerplate and runtime overhead than SvelteKit for the same result, and JSX takes getting used to.

python.description: My tool for scripting, data work, and anything where getting something running fast matters more than raw speed.
python.pro: Extremely readable and fast to write in, with an enormous library ecosystem for almost any task.
python.contra: Slow compared to compiled languages, and dynamic typing lets bugs slip through without discipline.

sql.description: The language I reach for whenever data has real structure and relationships worth enforcing.
sql.pro: Declarative and precise — the database figures out how to answer the question, not you.
sql.contra: Complex queries get hard to read fast, and schema migrations on live data need real care.

nosql.description: Useful when the data doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns, or the schema needs to stay flexible.
nosql.pro: Flexible schema and horizontal scaling make it a good fit for unstructured or fast-changing data.
nosql.contra: Weaker consistency guarantees by default, and enforcing structure has to happen in application code instead.

aws.description: My default cloud when a project needs real infrastructure — compute, storage, queues, all in one place.
aws.pro: Covers essentially every infrastructure need, with the maturity and reliability that comes from being first.
aws.contra: Pricing and IAM permissions are genuinely confusing, and it's easy to over-provision without noticing.

docker.description: How I make sure 'works on my machine' actually means something — every project ships in a container.
docker.pro: Consistent environments across dev, CI, and production, and it makes onboarding a new machine trivial.
docker.contra: Adds a layer of indirection to debug, and images can bloat fast without deliberate care.

kubernetes.description: For when Docker alone isn't enough — orchestrating containers at a scale that needs real automation.
kubernetes.pro: Self-healing, scriptable infrastructure that scales services up and down without manual intervention.
kubernetes.contra: Genuinely complex to operate — the learning curve and operational overhead are steep for small projects.

github-actions.description: My default CI/CD — tests, builds, and deploys run automatically on every push, right where the code lives.
github-actions.pro: Lives right next to the code, so pipelines are versioned with the repo and easy to review in a PR.
github-actions.contra: YAML config gets unwieldy fast for complex pipelines, and debugging a failing action can be slow.

vercel.description: Where I deploy most frontend projects — push to main and it's live, with previews on every PR.
vercel.pro: Zero-config deploys with instant preview URLs per branch — genuinely the fastest path from commit to live.
vercel.contra: Costs scale quickly past the free tier, and some platform-specific features create lock-in.

postgresql.description: My default relational database — solid, standards-compliant, and rarely the thing that goes wrong.
postgresql.pro: Rock-solid, standards-compliant SQL with rich extensions (JSONB, full-text search) most projects never outgrow.
postgresql.contra: Vertical scaling has real limits eventually, and tuning it well takes genuine operational knowledge.

redis.description: My go-to for caching and anything that needs to be fast and ephemeral — sessions, rate limits, queues.
redis.pro: Blazing fast in-memory operations make it ideal for caching, sessions, and simple pub/sub.
redis.contra: Data doesn't durably persist by default, and memory cost scales directly with dataset size.

sentry.description: How I actually find out something broke in production before a user has to tell me.
sentry.pro: Catches and contextualizes real production errors — stack traces, breadcrumbs, and the request that caused it.
sentry.contra: Noisy without tuning — needs real effort to filter signal from low-value alerts.
